nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name: Southern flounder
Scientific Name: Paralichthys lethostigma

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum: Chordata
      Class: Osteichthyes
      Order: Pleuronectiformes
      Family: Bothidae

nodes.title: Other Common Names
nodes.body:
Mud flounder, doormat, halibut (580); southern large flounder, fluke (232), saddleblanket.

Other:	Reference for Scientific Name (Jordan and Gilbert)

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  Southern flounder are fished commercially along its entire range; however landings data are often grouped with two other species (Paralichthys albigutta and P. dentatus). In the northwestern Gulf of Mexico, most southern flounder are caught incidentally in commercial shrimp trawls (791). Also caught with trammel nets, spears, and beach seines (791). Marketed mostly fresh (791).

Recreational: The southern flounder is a popular recreational species throughout its range. Fish are taken by hook-and-line and by gigging in shallow waters at night. Estimated recreational catch for Florida was 233,000 fish in 1990 (1363).

Ecological Role: The southern flounder is an important predator in estuarine ecosystems, feeding on small crustaceans, including penaeid shrimp, as juveniles and becoming piscivorous (179). Southern flounder have been introduced into freshwater reservoirs of Texas in an effort to control problem fish populations and improve recreational fishing (403 ) .

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  Paralichthys Lethostigma ranges from Albermarle Sound, North Carolina, southward to the Loxahatchee River, Florida, in the Atlantic and from the Caloosahatchee River Estuary, Florida, around the Gulf to northern Mexico (327).

Within Study Area: Occur on the Atlantic coast in northern Florida, and from the Caloosahatchee River northward on the Gulf coast (232 788 891 983). Rare south of Indian River and south of the Suwannee river, and absent in south Florida (788 983). Reported from Tampa Bay by Henshall (299), but Springer and Woodburn (664) stated that there are no other specimens known from that area. Christensen (887) considered the species uncommon in the Indian River Lagoon where he collected only 1 specimen.

Mobility and Migration:

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body:
Eggs float at or near the surface (21). Larvae are planktonic and can be found throughout the water column (379). King (379) has shown no difference between night and day larval distributions. Juveniles and adults are demersal; they are more active at night (566) .
Migrations and Movements:
Adults emigrate from the estuaries to spawn in deeper offshore waters during fall and winter; the migrations coincide with falling water temperatures (255 374 642). Males usually leave estuaries for the Gulf earlier than females (677). Hoese and Moore (327) report severe northers will result in mass emigrations, while moderate to warm winters cause flounders to leave the estuaries over longer periods of time. Stokes (677) indicates that only those fish emigrating are gravid. Some juveniles and adults overwinter in the deeper holes and channels of bays and estuaries (523 677 754). Postlarvae and juveniles immigrate into the bays and estuaries from late winter to spring. Williams and Deubler (769) indicated postlarval immigration correlates with lunar phase. In addition, adults migrate back into estuarine habitats throughout spring and into summer. Juveniles tend to migrate to low salinity water, often going up into river channels (769 561). Stokes (677) reported that local movements within and between estuaries rarely exceeded 18 km, but no consistent patterns were evident.

nodes.title: BENTHIC HABITAT
nodes.body:
Habitat Type: Eggs are marine, occurring in neritic waters. Early larval stages are marine, while postlarvae become estuarine. Juveniles and adults are estuarine, riverine and marine usually depending on size of the flounder and hydrography.
Substrate: Southern flounder frequent fine unconsolidated substrates and rarely occur on hard bottoms (566). Southern flounder have been commonly reported on mud, organic-rich muddy sand, and fine silty sand substrates (232 499 567 677 791 1376). Juvenile fish have been reported in association with seagrass beds (677). Adults prefer fine sediments associated with flooded Spartina marsh (677 754 787). Tabb and Manning (702) collected this species on shell sand and �rim marl bottoms off southwest Florida.

nodes.title: Physical/Chemical
nodes.body:
Temperature: Eurythermal, ranges and preferences, in parentheses, are:
eggs - 9.1 to 22.9 C, (14 C)
larvae - 2 to 30 C, (20-25 C)
juveniles - 2 to 31.2 C
adults - 5 to 34.9 C, (14 to 22 C) (561 754).
Temperature appears to have a greater affect on growth than salinity (555).
Salinity: Southern flounder are euryhaline (891); reported tolerances and preferences, in parentheses, are:
larvae - (10-30 ppt)
juveniles - 2-60 ppt (2-37 ppt)
adults - (3-60 ppt (20-30 ppt) (754).
Adults, while in estuarine situations, prefer the lower mixing and tidal fresh zones (255).  Found in freshwater in the St. Johns River, Florida (835) .
Dissolved Oxygen:  Deubler and Prosner (176) demonstrated avoidance behavior in juvenile southern flounder when dissolved oxygen levels fell below 3.7 mg/l, for temperatures 6.1, 14.4, and 25.3 C.

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body: Reproductive Mode: Fertilization is external, within the water column. The eggs float at or near the water surface (21 232).

nodes.title: Mating/Spawning
nodes.body:
Spawning occurs during late fall and early winter in marine neritic waters (614 580 232) with peak activity in Texas waters from Nov.-Jan, (255). A December peak reported in Louisiana (642). Spawning apparently occurs in water depths of 20-60m (47). In laboratory studies, Arnold et al. (21) reported that males attended females for a period of 3 weeks prior to spawning. At spawning, the females would swim to the surface and release eggs which were immediately fertilized by the attending male.
Fecundity: Individuals weighing from 1 to 3kg are reported to produce an average of 40,000 eggs/female (21). Nall (499) noted that all females over 6 years old had developing eggs.

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Eggs/Larvae: Diameter of unfertilized eggs is 0.92 mm (296). Laboratory spawned eggs hatch in 61-76 hours at 170 C and 28 ppt (21). Yolk-sac larvae, 40-46 days old and 8-11 mm long, begin metamorphosis into the postlarval stage; transformation is complete by about 50 days (21). Optimal growth in early postlarvae occurs at high salinities (175); while advanced postlarvae grow better at salinities of 5-15 ppt (676).
Juveniles/Adults: Minimum size of settled juveniles overlaps that of the postlarvae in some cases (10-15 mm TL). Peters (555) concluded P. lethostigma grows faster at warm temperatures and low salinities. On the basis of data provided by Stokes (6771, size estimated after the first and second year of growth is 201 and 250 mm TL for male, 225 and 364 mm TL for female southern flounder. The average total length of 2 year olds has been reported as 365mm (1014). Maturity reportedly occurs at 243 mm TL for females and at 170 mm TL for males (642), although Nall (499)stated that the smallest maturing female in his collection was 308mm TL. Nall (499) suggested a 9-10 year life-span, which is considerably greater than the 3-5 years reported by Stokes (677) and Manooch (1014). Females appear to grow faster, live longer, and attain greater size than males (677). Stokes (677) suggested that the maximum size for females is 620 mm TL and the maximum size of males is 320mm TL. Ginsburg (1376), however, reported a maximum size of 630mm, and others have given the maximum size as 750mm (791) to 760mm (788).

nodes.title: Trophic Modes
nodes.body: Southern flounder are carnivorous during all life stages. Larvae feed on zooplankton (555). Small crustaceans, particularly mysids, but also shrimp and crabs, make up the diet of small juveniles, 10-160 mrn TL (179 677 791). Larger juveniles and adults are basically piscivorous, feeding on small benthic and pelagic fishes, but shrimp, crabs and polychaetes are also utilized to a lesser extent (163 222 564 677 567 532).

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body: Paralichthys lethostigma and P. albigutta are very difficult to distinguish from each other during early life stages (775) . Early stages are often summarized as Paralichthys spp. (379) or just "southern flounder" (677). Adult southern flounder outnumber gulf flounder in the northern Gulf of Mexico and catches containing the two species are not usually separated. This makes catch data for the two species difficult to analyze.

nodes.body: Margot Hightower, Chief, NOAA, NMFS, Statistical Field Office, Galveston, Texas.
